# UNIT II: OPEN-SOURCE OPERATING SYSTEM — LINUX

**Total teaching hours:** 6  
**Study note:** Detailed explanations, comparison tables, embedded diagrams, command examples, practical procedures and real-world case studies.

> All diagrams are embedded directly in this Markdown file. No separate image files are required.

---

## Learning objectives

After completing this unit, students should be able to:

1. Explain the historical development of Unix and Linux.
2. Compare Linux, Unix and Windows operating systems.
3. Describe the major features, advantages and limitations of Linux.
4. Identify common Linux distributions and their use cases.
5. Explain the major layers of Linux architecture.
6. Describe Linux installation, disk partitioning and Logical Volume Manager (LVM).
7. Explain how to install Linux in a virtual machine and how containers run Linux applications.

# 2.1 Historical development of Linux and Unix

## What is an operating system?

An **operating system (OS)** is system software that manages computer hardware and provides services for application programs and users. It manages processor time, memory, files, storage devices, input/output devices, user accounts, networking and security.

Examples include Linux, Windows, macOS, Android and various Unix systems.

## What is Unix?

**Unix** is a family of operating systems that originated at AT&T Bell Laboratories in the late 1960s and early 1970s. It became influential because of its multiuser design, multitasking capabilities, portability and powerful command-line environment.

### Important Unix milestones

| Year / period | Development | Importance |
|---|---|---|
| 1969 | Early Unix development began at Bell Labs | Established the foundations of the Unix family |
| 1970s | Unix was rewritten in the C programming language | Improved portability across hardware |
| 1970s–1980s | Unix spread through universities and industry | Influenced operating-system design and tools |
| 1980s | BSD Unix and commercial Unix variants developed | Expanded networking and enterprise use |
| 1980s–1990s | POSIX standards emerged | Helped standardise interfaces across systems |

## What is Linux?

**Linux** is an open-source, Unix-like operating-system kernel created by Linus Torvalds in 1991. A complete Linux operating system normally combines the Linux kernel with system utilities, libraries, package-management tools and applications. Many distributions include GNU software, which is why the term **GNU/Linux** is also used.

### Important Linux milestones

| Year | Development | Importance |
|---|---|---|
| 1991 | Linus Torvalds announced work on a free operating-system kernel | Beginning of Linux kernel development |
| 1992 | Linux adopted GNU GPL version 2 | Enabled collaborative development under copyleft terms |
| Early 1990s | GNU tools and Linux kernel were combined in usable systems | Helped form complete GNU/Linux systems |
| 1993 | Debian and Slackware projects began | Important early distributions |
| 1994 | Linux kernel 1.0 was released | Major stable kernel milestone |
| 2000s | Linux became widely used on servers and embedded devices | Expanded enterprise and infrastructure adoption |
| 2010s onward | Linux became central to cloud and container infrastructure | Supports modern cloud-native environments |

![Unix and Linux historical timeline](data:image/png;base64,)

## Unix and Linux relationship

Linux was designed to behave like a Unix system, but it was not originally derived from proprietary Unix source code. It is commonly described as **Unix-like** because it follows many Unix design ideas and interfaces.

### Important terms

- **Unix:** historical operating-system family that began at Bell Labs.
- **Unix-like:** an operating system that follows Unix concepts and interfaces.
- **Linux kernel:** core component that manages hardware and system resources.
- **GNU:** project that created a large collection of free software tools and utilities.
- **GNU/Linux:** complete operating system combining the Linux kernel with GNU and other software components.
- **Distribution (distro):** packaged operating system built around the Linux kernel and selected software.

### Example

When a user installs Ubuntu, the user is not installing only the Linux kernel. Ubuntu provides the kernel, system libraries, command-line utilities, desktop environment (in desktop editions), package tools and other applications as an integrated operating system.

# 2.2 Comparison among Linux, Unix and Windows operating systems

Linux, Unix and Windows are operating-system families used in desktops, servers, workstations and specialised systems. Their licensing, architecture, administration tools and supported hardware differ.

| Basis | Linux | Unix | Windows |
|---|---|---|---|
| Origin | Linux kernel created by Linus Torvalds in 1991 | Began at AT&T Bell Labs | Developed by Microsoft |
| Source code | Mostly open source; individual components have their own licences | Depends on Unix system and vendor | Primarily proprietary |
| Licensing | Many distributions use open-source licences | Often commercial or vendor-specific; some BSD-derived systems are open source | Proprietary Microsoft licensing |
| User interface | CLI and graphical desktops | CLI and graphical interfaces, depending on system | Strong desktop GUI and command-line tools |
| Common shells / tools | Bash, Zsh, GNU tools | sh and other Unix shells | PowerShell, Command Prompt; WSL provides Linux environments |
| File systems | ext4, XFS, Btrfs and others | Depends on Unix variant | NTFS, ReFS and others |
| Software installation | Package managers and repositories | Vendor/package-specific tools | Installers, Microsoft Store, package managers |
| Customisation | Generally extensive | Depends on variant and vendor | More controlled by vendor and edition |
| Typical uses | Servers, cloud, embedded, desktop, supercomputing | Enterprise servers, workstations, specialised systems | Desktop, business systems, enterprise servers |
| Examples | Ubuntu, Fedora, Debian, RHEL | AIX, HP-UX, Solaris | Windows 11, Windows Server |

**Note:** macOS is Unix-certified, while Linux is generally Unix-like but is not itself a certified Unix operating system.

## Key differences explained

### 1. Licensing and source code

- Linux distributions are generally built from open-source components, although they may include proprietary drivers or applications.
- Commercial Unix systems may be distributed under vendor-specific licences.
- Windows is proprietary software, and users generally cannot modify its core source code.

### 2. Administration

Linux administration commonly uses terminal commands, configuration files and package managers. Windows administration commonly uses graphical tools, PowerShell and enterprise management platforms. Both systems can be administered remotely and automated.

### 3. Software installation

Linux example:

```bash
# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo apt update
sudo apt install nginx

# Fedora
sudo dnf install nginx
```

Windows example:

```powershell
# Install using winget, if available
winget install Mozilla.Firefox
```

### 4. File-system organisation

Linux uses a single directory tree starting at `/`. Windows commonly uses drive letters such as `C:\` and `D:\`.

---

# 2.3 Features and advantages of Linux

## Major features

1. **Open source:** most Linux distributions use open-source software licences, allowing inspection and modification according to licence conditions.
2. **Multiuser:** multiple user accounts can use the same system with separate permissions.
3. **Multitasking:** many processes can run concurrently.
4. **Portable:** Linux supports a wide range of processor architectures and devices.
5. **Security model:** users, groups, permissions, capabilities and security frameworks help control access.
6. **Networking:** includes tools and services for network communication and server administration.
7. **Shell and scripting:** automation can be performed using Bash, Python and other tools.
8. **File-system support:** supports many file systems, including ext4, XFS and Btrfs.
9. **Package management:** software can be installed and updated through repositories and package managers.
10. **Stability and scalability:** Linux is used in small embedded devices as well as large server and cloud environments.

## Advantages

- Flexibility and customisation.
- Reduced software licensing costs in many use cases.
- Strong server and networking capabilities.
- Access to a large software ecosystem.
- Automation through shell scripts and configuration tools.
- Wide hardware and architecture support.
- Community support and commercial support options.
- Useful learning environment for operating systems, networking, programming and cybersecurity.

## Limitations and challenges

- Some specialised commercial applications may not support Linux.
- Hardware drivers may vary by manufacturer and device.
- Beginners may need time to learn command-line administration.
- Different distributions use different package tools and configuration conventions.
- Poorly maintained systems can still be vulnerable.
- Enterprise deployment requires planning, training, support and patch management.

## Basic Linux commands

| Command | Purpose | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `pwd` | Show current directory | `pwd` |
| `ls` | List files | `ls -la` |
| `cd` | Change directory | `cd /etc` |
| `mkdir` | Create directory | `mkdir lab` |
| `touch` | Create empty file | `touch notes.txt` |
| `cp` | Copy files | `cp a.txt b.txt` |
| `mv` | Move or rename files | `mv old.txt new.txt` |
| `rm` | Remove files | `rm notes.txt` |
| `cat` | Display file content | `cat notes.txt` |
| `less` | Read a file page by page | `less /etc/os-release` |
| `whoami` | Show current user | `whoami` |
| `uname` | Show system information | `uname -a` |
| `df` | Show filesystem disk space | `df -h` |
| `free` | Show memory use | `free -h` |
| `ip` | Show network information | `ip addr` |
| `systemctl` | Manage services on systemd systems | `systemctl status ssh` |

### Example: create a small directory structure

```bash
mkdir linux-lab
cd linux-lab
mkdir notes commands backup
touch notes/unit2.txt
echo "Learning Linux" > notes/unit2.txt
cat notes/unit2.txt
ls -R
```

Expected structure:

```text
linux-lab/
├── backup/
├── commands/
└── notes/
    └── unit2.txt
```

### Understanding file permissions

Linux permissions are commonly represented by:

- `r` = read
- `w` = write
- `x` = execute

Example:

```bash
ls -l script.sh
chmod 755 script.sh
```

`755` means:
- Owner: read, write, execute.
- Group: read, execute.
- Others: read, execute.

Use `chmod` carefully. Granting broad write or execute permissions can create security risks.

# 2.4 Variants of Linux operating systems

A **Linux distribution** packages the Linux kernel with system utilities, libraries, software repositories, installation tools and often a desktop environment.

## Popular Linux distributions

| Distribution | Family / base | Common purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Ubuntu | Debian-based | Desktop, server, cloud and education |
| Debian | Independent community distribution | Stability and general-purpose computing |
| Linux Mint | Ubuntu / Debian-based editions | Beginner-friendly desktop |
| Fedora | Red Hat ecosystem | Developer workstation and new technologies |
| Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) | Red Hat ecosystem | Enterprise servers and support |
| Rocky Linux | RHEL-compatible ecosystem | Enterprise server environments |
| AlmaLinux | RHEL-compatible ecosystem | Enterprise server environments |
| Kali Linux | Debian-based | Penetration testing and security education |
| Arch Linux | Independent | Customisable, rolling-release systems |
| openSUSE | SUSE ecosystem | Desktop, server and administration |
| Alpine Linux | Independent, musl-based | Lightweight containers and minimal systems |

![Linux distribution families](data:image/png;base64,)

### 1. Debian family

Examples: Debian, Ubuntu and Linux Mint.

Common package format: `.deb`

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt upgrade
sudo apt install curl
sudo apt remove curl
```

### 2. Red Hat family

Examples: RHEL, Fedora, Rocky Linux and AlmaLinux.

Common package format: `.rpm`

```bash
sudo dnf check-update
sudo dnf upgrade
sudo dnf install httpd
sudo dnf remove httpd
```

### 3. Arch family

Example: Arch Linux. Common package manager: `pacman`.

```bash
sudo pacman -Syu
sudo pacman -S nginx
```

## How to select a Linux distribution

Consider purpose, support period, hardware, package ecosystem, community and vendor support, skill level, security and compliance requirements.

### Example choices

- Beginner learning Linux: Ubuntu or Linux Mint.
- Production enterprise server: a supported RHEL, Ubuntu LTS or other enterprise distribution.
- Security-testing lab: Kali Linux, used only in authorised environments.
- Lightweight container image: Alpine Linux, where application compatibility has been tested.

# 2.5 Overview of Linux architecture

Linux architecture describes how users, applications, system libraries, the kernel and hardware interact.

![Linux architecture](data:image/png;base64,)

## Main layers

### 1. Hardware layer

Physical components include CPU, RAM, hard disk or SSD, network interface cards, keyboard, display and other devices.

### 2. Kernel layer

The **Linux kernel** is the core of the operating system. It manages hardware resources and provides essential system services.

Major kernel responsibilities:

- **Process management:** creates, schedules and terminates processes.
- **Memory management:** allocates RAM and manages virtual memory.
- **Device management:** communicates with hardware through drivers.
- **File-system management:** provides a common interface to file systems.
- **Networking:** manages network protocols and packet processing.
- **Security:** supports access controls and other security mechanisms.

### 3. System libraries

Libraries provide reusable functions and interfaces for applications. For example, glibc is a common C library in many GNU/Linux distributions.

### 4. Shell and system utilities

A shell accepts commands and helps users interact with the system. Examples include Bash, Zsh and Fish. Common utilities include `ls`, `cp`, `grep`, `find`, `ps` and `systemctl`.

### 5. Application layer

Programs that users run include web browsers, text editors, database systems, web servers, development tools and office applications.

## Kernel space vs user space

| Kernel space | User space |
|---|---|
| Runs the kernel and privileged components | Runs ordinary applications and services |
| Has privileged access to hardware and memory | Applications have restricted access |
| Handles scheduling, memory and device operations | Applications request services through system calls |
| A kernel fault can affect the whole system | An application fault is often isolated to that application |

## What happens when Linux boots?

![Linux boot sequence](data:image/png;base64,)

1. **BIOS / UEFI:** firmware initialises hardware and selects a boot device.
2. **Bootloader:** commonly GRUB, loads the Linux kernel and initial RAM filesystem.
3. **Kernel:** initialises hardware, memory and core system facilities.
4. **Init system:** starts the first userspace process; many distributions use systemd.
5. **Services:** network, logging, login and other services start.
6. **User session:** the user reaches a command-line login or graphical desktop.

Useful commands:

```bash
uname -r
systemctl get-default
systemctl list-units --type=service
journalctl -b
```

## Linux file-system hierarchy

Linux organises files in a single tree beginning at `/`, called the root directory.

![Linux filesystem hierarchy](data:image/png;base64,)

| Directory | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `/` | Root of the directory tree |
| `/home` | Ordinary users' home directories |
| `/root` | Home directory of the root administrator |
| `/etc` | System-wide configuration files |
| `/var` | Variable data, such as logs and caches |
| `/usr` | Many user applications, libraries and shared data |
| `/bin` | Essential user commands; often linked to `/usr/bin` on modern systems |
| `/sbin` | System administration commands; often linked to `/usr/sbin` |
| `/boot` | Kernel and bootloader-related files |
| `/dev` | Device files |
| `/proc` | Virtual filesystem exposing process and kernel information |
| `/sys` | Virtual filesystem exposing device and kernel information |
| `/tmp` | Temporary files |
| `/mnt` | Common temporary mount point |
| `/media` | Common mount point for removable media |

# 2.6 Linux installation, disk partitioning and Logical Volume Manager (LVM)

## A. Before installing Linux

Before installation, identify the system purpose, processor architecture, RAM and disk requirements, network requirements, installation media, backup status, boot mode (UEFI or legacy BIOS), and disk layout.

**Warning:** partitioning and installation can erase data. Back up important files and verify the target disk before making changes.

## B. Linux installation workflow

![Linux installation steps](data:image/png;base64,)

### Example: installing Ubuntu Desktop

1. Download the official Ubuntu ISO image.
2. Verify the download using the published checksum where available.
3. Create a bootable USB using an appropriate tool, or attach the ISO to a virtual machine.
4. Boot the computer from USB or virtual DVD.
5. Select language, keyboard and installation options.
6. Select the installation destination and storage layout.
7. Create or confirm the user account and timezone.
8. Complete installation and reboot.
9. Remove the USB or detach the ISO when instructed.
10. Update the system and verify hardware and network operation.

After installation:

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt upgrade -y
sudo reboot
```

## C. Disk partitioning

A **disk partition** is a logically separated section of a physical storage device. An operating system can use partitions for different purposes.

Example disk:

```text
/dev/sda
├── /dev/sda1    EFI System Partition
├── /dev/sda2    Root filesystem
└── /dev/sda3    LVM physical volume
```

This is only an illustrative layout. Actual partition names and sizes depend on hardware, firmware and installation choices.

### Common Linux partitions

| Partition / mount point | Purpose |
|---|---|
| EFI System Partition (ESP) | Stores UEFI boot files; normally FAT32 |
| `/` | Root filesystem containing the operating system |
| `/home` | User data and personal configuration |
| `/boot` | Kernel and boot files, when a separate partition is used |
| Swap | Disk-backed memory area used under memory pressure or for hibernation when configured |

A separate `/home` partition is optional. Many installations use a single root filesystem with an EFI partition and swap file.

### Important disk terms

- **Disk:** physical storage device, such as an SSD.
- **Partition table:** records how a disk is divided.
- **GPT:** modern partition-table format commonly used with UEFI.
- **MBR:** older partition-table format with legacy limitations.
- **Filesystem:** defines how files and directories are stored, such as ext4 or XFS.
- **Mount point:** directory where a filesystem is made accessible.

### Useful disk commands

```bash
lsblk
sudo fdisk -l
df -h
sudo blkid
```

These commands help inspect disks, partitions, filesystems and mount points. Use read-only inspection commands before making changes.

### Example: understanding a partition

Suppose a computer has a 512 GB SSD:

| Partition | Example size | Purpose |
|---|---:|---|
| EFI | 512 MB | UEFI boot files |
| Root (`/`) | 100 GB | Linux system |
| Home (`/home`) | 350 GB | User files |
| Swap | 8 GB | Swap space |

These sizes are illustrative, not universal recommendations. Swap requirements depend on workload, RAM and hibernation needs.

## D. Logical Volume Manager (LVM)

**Logical Volume Manager (LVM)** is a Linux storage-management system that provides flexible storage allocation above physical disks or partitions.

Without LVM, changing partition sizes can be difficult. LVM makes it easier to allocate storage from a shared pool, subject to filesystem and operational constraints.

### LVM components

1. **Physical Volume (PV):** a disk or partition initialised for LVM.
2. **Volume Group (VG):** a storage pool made from one or more physical volumes.
3. **Logical Volume (LV):** a virtual block device allocated from a volume group.
4. **Filesystem:** created on a logical volume, for example ext4 or XFS.

![LVM structure](data:image/png;base64,)

### Simple LVM example

Assume a server has two spare disks or partitions:

```text
/dev/sdb1  ─┐
            ├── Volume Group: vg_data
/dev/sdc1  ─┘
                    ├── Logical Volume: lv_web
                    ├── Logical Volume: lv_database
                    └── Logical Volume: lv_backup
```

### LVM commands — conceptual lab example

**Warning:** The following commands can erase data on the selected devices. Do not run them on a real system until you have verified device names and backed up all important data. Use disposable virtual disks in a lab.

Inspect devices:

```bash
lsblk
sudo fdisk -l
```

Install LVM tools on Ubuntu / Debian:

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install lvm2
```

For a lab using two empty partitions, for example `/dev/sdb1` and `/dev/sdc1`:

```bash
# Initialise partitions as LVM physical volumes
sudo pvcreate /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1

# Create a volume group
sudo vgcreate vg_data /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1

# Create a 10 GB logical volume
sudo lvcreate -L 10G -n lv_web vg_data

# Create an ext4 filesystem
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/vg_data/lv_web

# Create a mount point
sudo mkdir -p /data/web

# Mount the logical volume
sudo mount /dev/vg_data/lv_web /data/web
```

Verify:

```bash
sudo pvs
sudo vgs
sudo lvs
lsblk
df -h
```

### Extend a logical volume

If the volume group has free space, a logical volume may be extended.

```bash
sudo lvextend -L +5G -r /dev/vg_data/lv_web
```

The `-r` option requests filesystem resizing as part of the operation when supported. Always verify filesystem type, free space and backup status first.

### Advantages of LVM

- Flexible storage allocation.
- Easier expansion when free space is available.
- Storage can be pooled from multiple physical volumes.
- Supports snapshots, subject to configuration and workload considerations.
- Useful for servers whose storage needs change over time.

### Limitations and cautions

- Adds administrative complexity.
- Does not replace backups.
- Snapshots are not a substitute for independent backup copies.
- Resizing rules differ between filesystems.
- A failed underlying disk can affect logical volumes unless suitable redundancy is configured.

# 2.7 Virtual machine and container installation

## A. What is a virtual machine?

A **virtual machine (VM)** is a software-based computer that runs its own guest operating system using virtualised hardware. A hypervisor manages the allocation of physical resources to virtual machines.

Examples include Oracle VirtualBox, VMware Workstation, Microsoft Hyper-V and KVM/QEMU.

![Virtual machines and containers](data:image/png;base64,)

### VM installation example using VirtualBox

1. Install VirtualBox on the host operating system.
2. Download an official Linux ISO image.
3. Create a new virtual machine.
4. Select Linux and the appropriate version.
5. Assign RAM and CPU cores within safe limits.
6. Create a virtual hard disk.
7. Attach the Linux ISO as a virtual optical disk.
8. Start the VM and follow the Linux installation steps.
9. Eject the ISO after installation.
10. Install guest additions or integration tools where appropriate.
11. Update the guest operating system.

### Example VM configuration for a basic Ubuntu lab

| Resource | Example allocation |
|---|---:|
| RAM | 4 GB |
| CPU | 2 virtual CPUs |
| Virtual disk | 30 GB |
| Network | NAT for basic internet access |
| ISO | Ubuntu Desktop or Server |

Actual requirements depend on the distribution, desktop environment and workload. Do not allocate more resources than the host can safely provide.

## B. What is a container?

A **container** packages an application and its dependencies into an isolated execution environment. Containers generally share the host operating-system kernel rather than running a separate guest kernel for every container.

Common container technologies include Docker Engine, containerd and Podman. Kubernetes is a container-orchestration platform, not itself a container runtime.

### VM vs container

| Basis | Virtual machine | Container |
|---|---|---|
| Operating system | Each VM normally runs a guest OS | Shares the host kernel |
| Size | Usually larger | Usually smaller |
| Startup | Often slower | Often faster |
| Isolation | Virtual hardware and guest OS boundary | Process and namespace-based isolation with kernel controls |
| Resource use | More overhead in many workloads | Often more lightweight |
| Kernel | Guest kernel per VM | Host kernel shared |
| Best suited for | Different OS environments and VM isolation | Packaging and deploying applications consistently |

**Important:** containers are not simply “small virtual machines.” They share the host kernel, so kernel compatibility and security configuration matter.

## C. Installing Docker on Ubuntu — example

The following is a learning example. For production, follow the official Docker Engine installation documentation for the exact Ubuntu release and verify repository and package instructions.

After installing Docker Engine using the official repository instructions, verify:

```bash
docker --version
sudo docker run hello-world
```

### Run a web server container

```bash
sudo docker run -d \
  --name linux-web-demo \
  -p 8080:80 \
  nginx
```

Explanation:

- `docker run`: creates and starts a container.
- `-d`: runs it in the background.
- `--name`: assigns a readable container name.
- `-p 8080:80`: maps host port 8080 to container port 80.
- `nginx`: image used to create the container.

Open this address in a browser on the host:

```text
http://localhost:8080
```

Useful commands:

```bash
sudo docker ps
sudo docker ps -a
sudo docker logs linux-web-demo
sudo docker stop linux-web-demo
sudo docker start linux-web-demo
sudo docker rm linux-web-demo
```

To remove the image after removing containers that use it:

```bash
sudo docker images
sudo docker rmi nginx
```

### Run an Ubuntu container

```bash
sudo docker run -it --name ubuntu-lab ubuntu:latest bash
```

Inside the container:

```bash
cat /etc/os-release
whoami
pwd
exit
```

The container provides an Ubuntu userland environment, but it uses the host's Linux kernel.

## D. VM and container use cases

| Requirement | Suitable approach |
|---|---|
| Learn a full Linux desktop without changing the host | Virtual machine |
| Test a different Linux distribution | Virtual machine |
| Run an isolated web application | Container |
| Package an application with dependencies | Container |
| Run Windows and Linux guest operating systems on one host | Virtual machine |
| Manage many containerised applications across multiple servers | Container platform such as Kubernetes |

# 3. Practical laboratory exercises

## Lab 1: Explore the Linux system

Run:

```bash
cat /etc/os-release
uname -a
hostname
whoami
pwd
lsblk
free -h
df -h
ip addr
```

**Tasks:**
1. Identify the Linux distribution and version.
2. Identify the running kernel version.
3. Identify the current username.
4. Find the available disk space.
5. Identify the network interface and IP address.

## Lab 2: File and directory management

```bash
mkdir -p ~/linux-practice/{documents,backup,scripts}
cd ~/linux-practice
touch documents/student.txt
echo "Linux practical exercise" > documents/student.txt
cp documents/student.txt backup/
mv backup/student.txt backup/student-copy.txt
ls -R
```

**Tasks:**
1. Create a directory named `college`.
2. Create two files inside it.
3. Copy one file to a backup directory.
4. Rename the copied file.
5. Display the content of the original file.

## Lab 3: Inspect storage

```bash
lsblk
df -h
sudo fdisk -l
sudo blkid
```

**Tasks:**
1. Identify the main disk.
2. List its partitions.
3. Identify the filesystem types.
4. Identify the mount point of the root filesystem.
5. Explain the difference between a disk, partition and filesystem.

## Lab 4: Virtual machine installation

**Tasks:**
1. Install VirtualBox or another approved hypervisor.
2. Download an official Ubuntu ISO.
3. Create a VM with suitable RAM, CPU and disk settings.
4. Install Ubuntu.
5. Log in and run `uname -a`.
6. Update the guest operating system.

## Lab 5: Container installation and test

After Docker Engine is installed:

```bash
sudo docker run -d --name web-lab -p 8081:80 nginx
sudo docker ps
```

**Tasks:**
1. Explain the purpose of `-d`.
2. Explain the port mapping `8081:80`.
3. Open `http://localhost:8081`.
4. View the container logs.
5. Stop and remove the container.

# 4. Real-world company case studies

These cases use publicly documented technologies and company activities as a foundation. The problem descriptions are instructional scenarios, not claims about confidential internal incidents.

## Case 1: Google — Linux and Kubernetes in large-scale infrastructure

**Public context:** Google contributed to open-source technologies including Kubernetes. Kubernetes originated from Google's experience with large-scale container management and was released as an open-source project in 2014.

### Problem scenario

A technology company operates hundreds of application services. Each service team deploys applications manually. When demand increases, administrators must configure more servers. Different environments create inconsistent deployments, and failed applications take time to recover.

### Linux-based approach

Use Linux servers as a common infrastructure platform and Kubernetes to orchestrate containerised applications.

### Proposed solution

1. Install a supported Linux distribution on server nodes.
2. Containerise applications and their dependencies.
3. Deploy workloads through Kubernetes.
4. Configure resource requests, limits and health checks.
5. Monitor node and application performance.
6. Apply operating-system and container security updates.

### Expected benefits

- Consistent application deployment.
- Automated workload scheduling.
- Better scaling and resource utilisation.
- Improved recovery and operational visibility.
- Reusable infrastructure practices.

### Questions

1. Why is Linux widely used in server infrastructure?
2. What is the difference between a Linux kernel and Kubernetes?
3. Why are containers useful for application deployment?
4. Does Kubernetes eliminate the need to maintain the underlying Linux servers?

**Reference:** Google Open Source — https://opensource.google/projects/kubernetes

## Case 2: Rackspace — OpenStack and Linux-based cloud infrastructure

**Public context:** Rackspace and NASA announced OpenStack in 2010. OpenStack is an open-source cloud-computing platform for managing compute, storage and networking resources.

### Problem scenario

A cloud provider wants to offer virtual machines to customers. Managing physical servers manually is becoming difficult. The provider needs a central platform to allocate compute, storage and network resources.

### Linux-based approach

Use Linux servers and OpenStack services to build and manage an Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) platform.

### Proposed solution

1. Install a supported Linux server distribution.
2. Configure networking and storage.
3. Deploy suitable OpenStack services.
4. Connect compute hosts to the cloud platform.
5. Provide controlled self-service access to customers.
6. Monitor capacity, security and availability.

### Expected benefits

- Centralised infrastructure management.
- Flexible allocation of compute resources.
- Better automation.
- Support for private and public cloud architectures.
- Collaboration through an open-source ecosystem.

### Questions

1. What is Infrastructure as a Service?
2. Why does a cloud provider need Linux servers?
3. What is the role of a hypervisor in OpenStack?
4. How are virtual machines different from containers?

**References:**
- OpenStack documentation — https://docs.openstack.org/
- Rackspace OpenStack overview — https://www.rackspace.com/library/what-is-openstack

## Case 3: Cisco — Linux, networking and open-source security tools

**Public context:** Cisco publishes open-source networking and security projects, including Snort and other projects in its open-source portfolio.

### Problem scenario

An enterprise has multiple office networks, Linux servers and cloud applications. Administrators have difficulty monitoring network traffic and identifying suspicious activity. They need tools that can be integrated into their security operations.

### Linux-based approach

Use Linux servers to host and operate suitable networking and security tools. Evaluate open-source network intrusion detection capabilities such as Snort.

### Proposed solution

1. Install a supported Linux distribution on a monitoring server.
2. Configure network interfaces and authorised traffic visibility.
3. Install and configure the selected monitoring or intrusion detection tool.
4. Define appropriate detection rules.
5. Forward alerts to the security monitoring workflow.
6. Update rules and software, and review alerts regularly.

### Expected benefits

- Better network visibility.
- Flexible monitoring configurations.
- Ability to inspect and adapt tools.
- Integration with existing security workflows.
- Practical learning in Linux networking and security.

### Questions

1. What is network intrusion detection?
2. Why might an organisation run monitoring tools on Linux?
3. Does installing Snort guarantee network security?
4. Why are updates, rules and skilled monitoring important?

**References:**
- Cisco Open Source — https://opensource.cisco.com/
- Snort — https://www.snort.org/

# 5. Integrated case study: College builds a Linux server lab

## Scenario

Lumbini Technical College has a computer laboratory with 40 desktop computers. Students study networking, programming, database management and cloud computing. The college currently depends on individual Windows installations and has no dedicated Linux server environment.

The ICT department wants to establish a practical lab where students can learn Linux administration, web hosting, virtualisation, storage management and containers.

The college has one server with 16 CPU cores, 64 GB RAM and 2 TB storage. It plans to use Ubuntu Server, virtual machines and Docker for laboratory exercises.

## Problems identified

1. Students have limited practical Linux experience.
2. There is no centralised Linux server.
3. Storage is not organised for flexible expansion.
4. Students cannot safely experiment on production systems.
5. Web applications are deployed inconsistently.
6. The college needs a manageable backup and security process.

## Proposed solution

| Problem | Proposed solution | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Limited Linux knowledge | Ubuntu Server training environment | Provides hands-on Linux administration |
| No server platform | Install Linux on the physical server | Provides a common lab platform |
| Flexible storage requirement | Evaluate LVM | Allows logical storage allocation and expansion |
| Risk to production system | Use virtual machines | Provides separate guest environments |
| Inconsistent application deployment | Use containers | Packages applications and dependencies |
| Data-loss risk | Configure backups and test restoration | Protects student work and system data |
| Security risks | Apply updates, access controls and monitoring | Improves system security |

## Suggested architecture

```text
                  College Computer Lab
                          |
                    Campus Network
                          |
                 Linux Physical Server
                          |
                  Hypervisor / KVM
                          |
              +-----------+-----------+
              |           |           |
           VM 1         VM 2        VM 3
        Ubuntu Lab   Database Lab  Network Lab
              |
        Docker Engine
              |
       +------+------+
       |             |
    Web App       Test App
   Container     Container
```

## Implementation steps

**Step 1 — Prepare the server:** check hardware compatibility, back up existing data and plan storage.

**Step 2 — Install Linux:** install a supported Ubuntu Server release and configure network access.

**Step 3 — Configure storage:** create a suitable partition layout and use LVM if flexible storage allocation is required.

**Step 4 — Configure virtualisation:** install and configure a hypervisor such as KVM/QEMU.

**Step 5 — Create lab VMs:** create separate virtual machines for Linux, databases and networking practice.

**Step 6 — Install containers:** install Docker Engine or another approved container runtime in a lab VM.

**Step 7 — Apply security:** configure user permissions, firewall rules, updates, backups and monitoring.

**Step 8 — Test:** verify access, performance, recovery and student isolation.

## Assessment questions

1. Why is Linux suitable for a college server lab?
2. What is the difference between a Linux distribution and a Linux kernel?
3. Why might the college use LVM?
4. Explain the difference between a physical server and a virtual machine.
5. Why should students use virtual machines for experiments?
6. What is the advantage of using containers for web applications?
7. Identify four basic Linux commands useful to a system administrator.
8. What security measures should be implemented?
9. What is the role of a hypervisor?
10. Draw and explain the proposed college lab architecture.

# 6. Quick revision notes

- **Operating system:** software that manages hardware and provides services to applications.
- **Unix:** operating-system family originating at Bell Labs.
- **Linux:** open-source, Unix-like kernel created by Linus Torvalds in 1991.
- **Distribution:** Linux kernel packaged with utilities, libraries, tools and applications.
- **Kernel:** core component managing processes, memory, devices, filesystems and networking.
- **Shell:** command interpreter used to interact with the operating system.
- **Ubuntu:** Debian-based Linux distribution.
- **RHEL:** enterprise Linux distribution from Red Hat.
- **Partition:** logical division of a physical disk.
- **Filesystem:** structure used to organise files and directories.
- **LVM:** flexible storage-management layer using PVs, VGs and LVs.
- **PV:** Physical Volume.
- **VG:** Volume Group.
- **LV:** Logical Volume.
- **VM:** software-based computer with virtual hardware and a guest operating system.
- **Container:** isolated application environment sharing the host kernel.
- **Hypervisor:** software layer that creates and manages virtual machines.
- **Docker:** platform and tooling for building and running containers.
- **Kubernetes:** platform for orchestrating containerised applications.
